targets.canonical_target: The observable criteria, signals, or diagnostic methods available to a user for distinguishing retained internal state from externally reconstructed context, given that the two mechanisms can produce similar behavior.

An enumeration of the concrete mechanisms by which prior-interaction information is supplied externally at generation time (e.g., saved summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history), as distinct from retained internal state.
The means, if any, by which an external user could distinguish retained internal state from externally supplied context as the source of observed continuity across interactions.
A comparative effect claim: how response accuracy and consistency differ when continuity comes from externally reconstructed history versus retained full internal context.

The observable means or diagnostic criteria (if any) by which a user could distinguish continuity produced by retained internal state from continuity produced by externally supplied context at runtime.

An enumeration of the concrete external mechanisms or techniques by which prior-interaction information is supplied at runtime (e.g., saved summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history), i.e., the specific means of reconstructing access rather than retained internal state.

The methods, evidence, or diagnostic criteria (beyond observable response behavior) that would discriminate whether continuity across generations arises from retained internal state versus externally supplied context at runtime.

Methods or diagnostic criteria that could discriminate between a system retaining internal state across interactions versus a fresh process reconstructing continuity from externally supplied records, given that their observable outputs can coincide.

An enumeration of the types/forms of externally supplied continuity artifacts (e.g., saved summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) that can serve as reconstructed access to prior-exchange information.

A comparison of response quality/accuracy outcomes between retained full internal context and externally reconstructed context, i.e., whether and how much performance differs between the two mechanisms.

Whether any output-only method exists that reliably discriminates internally persisted context from externally supplied reconstructed context, and what such a discriminating procedure or signature would be.

A comparison of how dependably and faithfully retained internal state versus externally reconstructed context (summaries, retrieved records, user-supplied history) reproduce details of an earlier interaction, including their respective failure modes and sources of error.

Whether any output-only diagnostic criterion exists that lets an external observer determine which of two underlying continuity mechanisms (retained internal state vs. fresh process supplied with an external record) produced a response, given that both can yield identical outward behavior.

Whether and by what response-based diagnostic criteria an external observer can tell retained internal state apart from a fresh process supplied with external context, given that both can produce the same outward behavior.

A comparison of the accuracy/fidelity of prior-interaction information as reconstructed from external sources (summaries, retrieved records, user-supplied history) versus as preserved in full retained internal context, i.e., whether and how the reconstructed version is lossy, distorted, or equivalent.

The mechanistic difference between prior information persisting as the system's own carried-over internal state versus being re-supplied at runtime from external sources (summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history), despite both producing similar continuity behavior.
The mechanism (or its absence) by which a generating system internally discriminates the provenance of available information — retained internal state versus externally supplied context at runtime.

The mechanism or process by which externally supplied continuity (saved summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) is fed into a new generation to restore access to earlier information, as distinct from retained internal state.

Specific diagnostic methods or observations (technical tests, instrumentation, or experimental procedures) that would reliably discriminate whether an AI system's cross-interaction continuity arises from internal persistent state versus externally supplied reconstructed context.

The types/categories of externally supplied context artifacts (e.g., saved summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) that can furnish continuity to a fresh generation lacking internal state.

The set of methods or diagnostic techniques capable of reliably discriminating between retained internal state and externally supplied context as the source of an AI system's apparent continuity across interactions.

An enumeration of the types/categories of external continuity artifacts (e.g., saved summaries, retrieved records, user-supplied history) that can be supplied at runtime and drawn on by a later response to reconstruct earlier-interaction context.

A comparison of the two continuity mechanisms (externally supplied/reconstructed prior information vs. retained internal state) along two specific dimensions: their privacy implications and their reliability/fidelity in preserving prior-exchange information.

Methods or diagnostic criteria capable of discriminating internal persistence of context from externally supplied reconstruction, given that observable outputs underdetermine which mechanism is operating.
The arbitration policy or weighting mechanism an AI service uses to resolve conflicts between retained internal state and externally supplied prior information when both are present.

Whether and how the two continuity mechanisms (persisted internal state vs. externally injected context) can be told apart from outward behavior alone, i.e., the existence and nature of behavioral discriminating criteria between them.

Whether and how output-only observation can discriminate retained internal state from externally supplied context reconstruction — i.e., the existence and nature of a reliable behavioral discriminator between the two mechanisms given identical observable responses.
The methods or evidence, beyond observable output behavior, by which an external observer could distinguish internally persisted continuity from externally supplied reconstruction of context.

Experimental methods or test designs that could discriminate whether cross-turn continuity arises from internal state persistence versus externally supplied reconstructed context, given that observable outputs alone are insufficient.
Whether any dependable method exists for distinguishing internally persisted context from externally supplied reconstruction as the source of continuity across generations.

The behavioral discriminants or diagnostic criteria, if any, that would let an outside observer tell retained internal state apart from externally supplied context using only observable outputs of the service.

The mechanism or internal criterion by which a system could tell apart information carried over from retained internal state versus information supplied externally at runtime (summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) during generation.
A method or criterion (beyond observable output behavior) that would reliably discriminate internally persisted continuity from externally reconstructed continuity.

The design consequences that follow from treating retained internal state versus externally supplied context records as distinct architectures for maintaining conversational coherence — i.e., what differs practically (engineering tradeoffs, requirements, or choices) between the two, rather than how to tell them apart from behavior.

A comparative evaluation of fidelity — how accurate and relevant externally supplied continuity (summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) is relative to information held in retained full internal state across generations.

The diagnostic criteria, tests, or observable signatures that would discriminate between continuity produced by externally supplied records at runtime and continuity produced by retained internal state.

The defining difference in mechanism between continuity arising from persistent internal state carried over from an earlier interaction and continuity reconstructed by supplying an external record to a fresh process, given that both can produce similar outward behavior.
The means or criteria available to a user for distinguishing internally persisted context from externally supplied reconstruction, given that observable outputs are consistent with both.
Methods or diagnostic procedures by which an observer could distinguish internally persisted context from externally supplied/reconstructed context in an AI system.

A comparative performance judgment between the two continuity mechanisms (retained internal state vs. externally reconstructed prior information) with respect to accuracy/reliability of subsequent responses — i.e., whether one systematically outperforms the other rather than merely producing similar behavior.

A comparative characterization of how context fidelity — accuracy and completeness of prior-interaction information — differs when it is reconstructed from external sources (summaries, retrieved records, user-provided history) versus retained as full internal state, i.e., what information is degraded, lost, distorted, or preserved under each mechanism.

Investigative or diagnostic methods (beyond observing output behavior) capable of reliably determining whether cross-turn continuity arises from retained internal state versus externally supplied context.

Whether and how retained internal state versus externally supplied context can be told apart from response behavior alone — i.e., the existence and nature of an observable discriminating criterion available to an outside observer.

Whether any reliable method exists for determining, for a given response, whether its continuity arose from internal persistence or external reconstruction — i.e., the existence (or nonexistence) of a discriminating test between the two sources.

The comparative effect of external summary fidelity (quality/completeness) on later-response accuracy relative to accuracy achievable with full retained internal state — i.e., how degradation or richness of the external record changes response correctness versus the retained-state baseline.
